claims.text: A shell reads a command line, splits it into words, treats the first word as the name of what to run, and passes the remaining words on as arguments; words holding no character the shell acts on (such as `*` or `>`) arrive at the program unchanged.
claims.source_hint: Bash Reference Manual, 'Shell Operation' and 'Simple Commands'

claims.text: Before searching for a program file, the shell checks whether the first word names something it carries out itself (a shell built-in); in bash `cd` is a built-in, while `ls`, `cat`, `mkdir`, `cp`, `mv`, `rm`, `wc` and `head` are program files.
claims.source_hint: Bash Reference Manual, 'Command Search and Execution'; 'Shell Builtin Commands'

claims.text: `cd` is a shell built-in and changes the working directory of the shell itself, printing nothing when it succeeds; a separate program could change only its own working directory, which would be gone when it exits.
claims.source_hint: Bash Reference Manual, 'Bourne Shell Builtins' (cd); POSIX rationale for cd as a built-in

claims.text: When the first word is not a built-in, the shell searches for an executable file of that name in a list of directories it keeps, starts it, and waits for it to finish before reading the next line.
claims.source_hint: Bash Reference Manual, 'Command Search and Execution'; 'Job Control' (foreground)

claims.text: `pwd`, `ls`, `cd`, `cat`, `mkdir`, `cp`, `mv` and `rm` are standard on Linux and macOS machines and inside a bash terminal on Windows; they are separate programs or shell built-ins, not features of a particular terminal application.
claims.source_hint: POSIX.1 Shell and Utilities, chapter 'Utilities' (ls, cat, mkdir, cp, mv, rm, pwd, cd); GNU coreutils manual

claims.text: In bash (the shell Git Bash opens and the one the lab box runs), Tab completes a partly typed name from the names in the current folder; if none starts with the text, or several do, nothing is filled in. A folder completes by name even if the user may not enter it.
claims.source_hint: Bash Reference Manual, 'Readline Interaction' / 'Commands For Completion' (complete, TAB)

claims.text: Bash keeps a history of the lines entered in the session, and the Up arrow recalls previously entered lines.
claims.source_hint: Bash Reference Manual, 'Bash History Facilities'; Readline 'Commands For History' (previous-history)

claims.text: `ls -1` prints one entry per line; when more than one directory is given as an operand, `ls` prints each with its name as a heading and separates the groups with a blank line.
claims.source_hint: POSIX.1 utility 'ls', options -1 and operand handling; GNU coreutils manual, 'ls invocation'

claims.text: `wc -l db/schema.sql` prints the line count followed by the file name it was given; at tag stage-0 the captured output is `48 db/schema.sql`.
`head -2 <file>` prints the first two lines of that file and nothing else.

`echo` with no arguments prints an empty line; the blank lines that separate the blocks of the captured output come from those calls, while the blank lines inside the `ls` listing are printed by `ls` between one directory's group and the next.
`..` names the directory one level up, so `cd db/queries` followed by `cd ../..` returns the run to where it started, which the two `pwd` lines of the output show.
`pwd` prints the working directory of the run that calls it.
claims.source_hint: POSIX.1 utility 'pwd'; Bash Reference Manual, 'Bourne Shell Builtins' (pwd)

claims.text: In the example repository at tag stage-0, most lesson scripts under `scripts/` — including `scripts/terminal/tour.sh` — carry a line near the top that starts the same file again inside the lab box, so their output is the same on Windows, macOS, Linux and CI.

The lab box that `scripts/up.sh` starts runs on the reader's own machine with its own paths and its own shell; `up.sh` makes the reader's example folder visible inside it at `/repo`, which is why `tour.sh` prints `/repo` and lists the same `db`, `docs`, `www`.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang docker-compose.yml, service `lab` (volume mount of the repository at /repo)

claims.text: Installing Git on Windows adds a terminal window called Git Bash, which runs bash, so no other install is needed; in it a Windows folder such as `C:\Users\you` is written `/c/Users/you`.
claims.source_hint: Git documentation / Git for Windows installation notes (Git Bash)

claims.text: Opinion, stated with its condition: when you need to repeat what you did or hand it to someone else exactly, a typed line is easier to keep and send than a sequence of clicks.

Opinion, stated with its condition: when a name refuses to complete on Tab, the most common cause is that the run is standing somewhere the name does not exist; for `cd` it can also mean the matching name is a file rather than a folder.

Some words are changed by the shell before the program sees them: a word containing `*` is replaced with the file names it matches, and `>` is kept by the shell to send the output to a file instead of reaching the program as an argument.
When the first word of a command line contains a `/`, the shell does not search its list of directories: it runs exactly the file that path names, which is how `scripts/terminal/tour.sh` runs.
claims.source_hint: Bash Reference Manual, 'Command Search and Execution' (first step: a slash in the command name)

claims.text: At tag stage-0, `scripts/up.sh` prints the line `The lab is up.` once the lab is started, so the reader can tell the lab box is ready before running a lesson script.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang scripts/up.sh at stage-0 (echo lines after docker compose up --wait)
